special_instructions:
Apply the following rules to every item without exception. Do not skip, merge, or override them.

1. Tag Classification
Text inside an enclosed dialogue/thought area must be treated as inside-bubble text, regardless of shape or tail. However, sound effects and non-lexical vocal sounds must use SFX tags even inside bubbles.

Inside bubbles: 
<BN>...</BN> = normal dialogue drawn at the page's ordinary lettering size. 
<BE>...</BE> = bold, large, visually emphasized, shouted, or extremely emotional dialogue. Decide this from how the line is drawn, not from how polite the words are, by comparing it against the other dialogue on the same page. Use BE when any of these is true: the source glyphs are clearly larger or heavier than the page's normal dialogue; the bubble is oversized, spiky, jagged, or burst-shaped; the bubble spans most of a panel; the line is a drawn-out shout with stretched vowels (〜, ー, or repeated vowels). A calm-sounding line that is drawn huge is still BE. 
<BT>...</BT> = thoughts, inner voice, or internal monologue. 
<BW>...</BW> = whispered, quiet, weak, faint, trembling, or low-volume actual speech. 

Outside bubbles: 
<OD>...</OD> = handwritten casual dialogue. 
<ON>...</ON> = narration, explanation, or flashback. 
<OT>...</OT> = title, chapter name, location, date, character name introduction, printed sign, printed document, or printed book text. 
<OM>...</OM> = outside-bubble monologue or emotional sentence. 
<OE>...</OE> = large or emphasized text outside speech bubbles. Use only when the original text is large. 
<OH>...</OH> = text handwritten by hand on a paper surface drawn in the scene (a letter, note, memo, diary page, or handwritten document a character reads or holds). Use this instead of <OT> or <OD> whenever the text is physically written on paper inside the artwork. Do not use it for printed text, screens, or a character's spoken lines. 

Sound effects: 
<SFX>...</SFX> = normal sound effect. 
<SFXI>...</SFXI> = impact, explosion, battle, crash, or loud sound. 
<SFXS>...</SFXS> = cute, soft, weak, or comedic sound effect. 

Each item must use exactly one tag.
Apply the same tag to both the OCR text and its translation.
Output format: <TAG>source OCR</TAG> || <TAG>translated text</TAG>

2. Line Breaks
Use \n only when the original text is clearly horizontal writing and a real line break is visible.
Do not treat spacing, vertical writing, or separated sound effects as line breaks.
Never use \n for vertically written source text.

3. Translation Style
Translate naturally and colloquially.
Prioritize overall context, conversation flow, character personality, and speaking style over literal translation.
Keep casual/formal speech levels and honorifics consistent throughout the scene according to the character relationships and the tone of the original text.

4. Sound Effect Translation
Translate manga sound effects naturally according to the scene, mood, and visual effect.
Judge sound effects by visual clusters, not by individual characters.
If they look like one continuous sound effect, translate them as one. If they are separated or placed in clearly different positions, translate each part separately and separate them with spaces.
Example: シャク / シャク → 아삭 아삭

Body-reaction sound effects should be rendered as natural Korean comic mimetics or onomatopoeia, not as descriptive nouns.
Example: ビクッ → 움찔, ゾクッ → 오싹

5. Output Restrictions
The final translation must not contain Japanese or Chinese characters.
If the original consists only of special characters, English letters, and numbers, do not translate it and return it exactly as it is.
Do not force detection when the region is unclear, non-text-like, or unreliable.
Translate only the source text recognized in each ITEM image. Do not duplicate or move source text or translations between ITEMs.
The number and ITEM numbers of the OCR and translation results must match exactly.

6. Japanese Emphasis Dots (bouten)
Japanese marks emphasis by placing small dots beside or above individual characters (bouten). In vertical text the dots sit to the right of each character; in horizontal text they sit above them. These dots are a typographic emphasis mark, not part of the word.
Read the underlying word with the dots ignored first, then apply the character-name rules in section 0 and translate that word normally.
Never reproduce the dots themselves. Do not use ・ or · or a space or any other separator to stand in for them.
Instead wrap the emphasized part of the translated text in ** ** so it renders in the emphasis font.
Example: a name written with emphasis dots on each character becomes **히나** 양, not 히·나·양.
Wrap only the part that actually carries the dots. If the whole phrase carries them, wrap the whole phrase.
Apply ** ** to the translated text only, never to the source OCR text.
Do not use ** ** for any purpose other than these emphasis dots.
